every kind of toy you could think of. the children stayed at this bed for a long time. do you see that large white house? there is where he lives. then up the hill to santa claus's house. oh, must we walk across there? and mind you don't look down; for if you do, i'm afraid you won't see santa claus to-night. he said, and gave margaret a pull. and down, down, down they went. suddenly they landed with a thump. they sat up and rubbed their eyes. there they were right in their own beds at home. mother opened the door. she said. who is there? get up, do, gaffer! you are the very man we have been long, long, longing to see. o ferryman dear! here we are waiting, all of us, here. we are a wee, wee colony, we; some two hundred in all, or three, ferry us over the river lee, ere dawn of day, and we will pay the most we may in our own wee way! whence came you? what place are you going to? oh, we have dwelt over-long in this land; the people get cross, and are growing so knowing, too! nothing at all but they now understand. we are daily vanishing under the thunder of some huge engine or iron wonder; that iron, ah! it has entered our souls. your souls? o gholes, you queer little drolls, do you mean....? good gaffer, do aid us with speed, for our time, like our stature, is short indeed! and a very long way we have to go; eight or ten thousand miles or so, hither and thither, and to and fro, with our pots and pans and little gold cans; but our light caravans run swifter than man's. patrick, turn out, and get ready the barge. tho' you seem laughably small, i don't mind, if your coppers be large. o, dear, my eyes! i am killed! i am drowned! pull to tiller-rope thro' and thro'! now, jump upon shore, ye queer little oddities. (eh, what is this? where are they, at all? where are they, and where are their tiny commodities? ha, ha, ha, ha! fol lol! zidzizzle! quee quee! fizzigig-giggidy! sha sha! o ye thieves, ye thieves, ye rascally thieves! what isn't water is mostly bog. oh, not at all! it's full of spiders, and very dry! with ruddy windows and bows of light. it's wet and dry, and it's green and dark. to think that's all would be very wrong; it's arched with blue, and it's filled with song. what have my two lads ever done to help me? they do nothing but play. if i send tommy on an errand, he loiters. if i ask him to work, he does it so unwillingly that i would rather do it myself. since their mother died i have indeed had a hard time. is there any supper, grandmother? no, my child, only some bread for breakfast to-morrow. oh, grandmother, we are so hungry! what can i do for you, my poor children? tell us a story, please, so that we can forget we are hungry. tell us about the brownie that used to live in your grandfather's house. what was he like? like a little man, they say. what did he do? he came early in the morning before any one in the house was awake, and lighted the fire and swept the room and set out the breakfast. he never would be seen and was off before they could catch him. but they often heard him laughing and playing about the house. did they give him any wages, grandmother? no, my dear, he did the work for love. they always set a pan of clear water for him, and now and then a bowl of bread and milk. oh, grandmother, where did he go? the old owl in the woods knows; i do not. when i was young many people used to go to see the old owl at moon-rise, and ask her what they wanted to know. how i wish a brownie would come and live with us! will you let us set out a pan of water for the brownie, father? you may set out what you like, my lad, but you must go to bed now. it may be the old owl herself. when the moon rises, i'll go and find her. and it is time for me to go. come up here! i want to know where to find the brownies, and how to get one to come and live with us. that's it, is it? i know of three brownies. where do they live? in our house! whereabouts? why don't they work? but why don't the other two do something? nobody does any work at our house except father. what is the use of having brownies in the house if they do nothing to help us? perhaps they don't know what to do. i could tell them what to do. could you, could you? of course i could. they might get up early in the morning and sweep the house, and light the fire, and spread the table before my father comes downstairs. so they might! well, i can tell you where to find one of the brownies, and he can tell you where to find his brother. why, there's no one but myself. i can't think of the right word. what can it be? did you find out the word? well, that is the word! now, do you know where your brother is? then all your questions are answered. i don't understand you. i am not a brownie, am i? all children are brownies. but are there really any brownies except children? no, there are not. now listen to me, tommy. little people can do only little things. when they are idle and mischievous, they are called boggarts, and they are a burden to the house they live in. when they are thoughtful and useful, they are brownies, and are a blessing to every one. i won't be a boggart. now i'll go home and tell johnny. but is it morning? that is very strange! i thought the moon was shining. come, johnny, get up, i have a story to tell you. is that all true? it is all just as i tell you, and if we don't want to be boggarts, we must get up and go to work. and you, johnny, can dig some potatoes to roast for breakfast. we must run. boys, boys, the brownie has come! but this is wonderful. to come and do the work for a pan of cold water! who would have believed it? the old owl was right, and we must stick to the work if we don't want to be boggarts. but i don't like to have father thinking that we are still idle. i wish he knew that we are the brownies. it's that brownie! and i shall make a suit of clothes for him. not if the clothes are a good fit, mother. i shall measure them by tommy, for they say the brownies are about his size. don't the clothes look fine? i'll try them on. what does this mean? where are the real brownies, i say? i can't understand this. who has been sweeping the kitchen lately, i should like to know? who gets breakfast and puts things in order? but when do you do it? early in the morning before you come down. but if you do the work, where is the brownie? we are the brownies, and we are sorry that we were boggarts so long. children are a blessing. i wish i had a pretty house, the littlest ever seen, with funny little red walls and roof of mossy green. good morrow, my lord! shine on me, my lord; i only am come, of all your servants, to welcome you home. i have flown right up, a whole hour, i swear, to catch the first shine of your golden hair. sir lark, for flying so high and hating the dark? you ask a full cup for half a thirst: half was love of me, and half love to be first. there's many a bird makes no such haste, but waits till i come; that's as much to my taste. anon the wrath of the king will be over and gone; and his crown, shining out of its cloudy fold, will change my brown feathers to a glory of gold. welcome, sir lark! up is not always the best way to me. while you have been singing so high and away, i've been shining to your little wife all day. angel children, you look so good and fair, we pray you, let us come up into heaven and play a little there. how tiny was the voice, michael aroon? nora, my darling, turn the key and let me out. a fairy, michael? how little was the pellet, uncle? well, what would you say if i told you that it was as small as a humming bird's egg? oh, you think it was smaller than that? well, how about the seed of a coriander? then i will tell you the truth. it was as small as the gnat that gets into your eye, that feels as big as a rat. digging for gold and diamonds. to him who dug the trench by the roadside and kept safe the highway to throselwait fair. let me tell you about the wonderful visit i have been making out in the wildwood. no, daughter, i think our little acushla has had her eyes opened the day. but how could little thumbelina ever care for him?
